note: Site dates for Karnak (Precinct of Amun-Ra). Years BC are negative. Reign dates follow Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000); other chronologies differ by up to about 25 years for the New Kingdom. Survey draft of 22 November 2026: research fills in who, events and links, and checks every date.
owners: the Eleventh Dynasty kings of Thebes, whose earliest known monument here is a column of Intef II naming Amun-Ra
the Twelfth and Thirteenth Dynasty kings, with the temple run by Amun's priests
the Theban kings of the Seventeenth Dynasty, while the Hyksos ruled the north
the New Kingdom pharaohs, with the temple and its vast lands (the Estate of Amun) run by the High Priest of Amun
Akhenaten, who built temples to the Aten here and then closed Amun's temples and had his name hacked out
the restored cult under Tutankhamun, Horemheb and the Ramesside kings, with the High Priests of Amun growing ever more powerful
the High Priests of Amun, who ruled Upper Egypt from Thebes in the Twenty-first Dynasty
the Libyan kings of the Twenty-second and Twenty-third Dynasties, who made their sons High Priests of Amun
the Kushite kings of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, through the God's Wife of Amun
the Saite kings of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, after the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 664 BC, through the God's Wife of Amun
the Persian kings (the Twenty-seventh Dynasty)
the last native kings, the Twenty-eighth to Thirtieth Dynasties, then briefly the Persians again
Alexander the Great and then the Ptolemies, the Macedonian kings of Egypt
the Roman emperors; the temple declined and Thebes shrank to villages
the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) emperors; pagan worship had been banned, and Christians built churches in the ruins
the Islamic rulers of Egypt, from the Arab conquest to the Mamluks; the village of Karnak grew among the ruins
Ottoman Egypt (with the French occupation of 1798–1801), when travellers, collectors and early scholars visited and removed objects
the Egyptian Antiquities Service, founded by Auguste Mariette and run by French directors until 1952; from 1967 with the Franco-Egyptian Centre (CFEETK)
the Egyptian Antiquities Organisation
the Supreme Council of Antiquities
the Ministry of Antiquities (Ministry of State for Antiquities at first)
the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, through the Supreme Council of Antiquities, with the CFEETK for research and restoration
